Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, announced on his website that he believes he has proved the Riemann hypothesis using the large language model Claude.
He said the proof was completed late Sunday night and that he delayed public release until after Anthropic’s IPO on Thursday.
The claim has not been independently verified and Anthropic has not commented on the result.
Alpöge’s proof was written in the Lean proof assistant and extends to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, with a suggestion it could also address the Extended Riemann Hypothesis given more time.
The Riemann hypothesis is one of the seven Millennium Prize problems, each carrying a $1 million prize from the Clay Mathematics Institute.
Anthropic previously noted in August that it was experimenting with Claude on the problem but did not expect the model’s techniques to yield a proof.
The claim remains a draft on Alpöge’s site and has not been submitted for formal acceptance by the Institute.
The Riemann hypothesis, first proposed in 1859, concerns how the non‑trivial zeroes of the Riemann zeta function relate to the distribution of prime numbers, a central question in number theory.
Solving it would be a historic breakthrough, as it has resisted proof by the world’s leading mathematicians for decades.
Claude, Anthropic’s conversational AI, has been used in earlier mathematical experiments, but this is the first public claim of a full proof generated with its assistance.
Anthropic's Claude claims proof of Riemann hypothesis, shaking math world.

Google has replaced the traditional Search button on its desktop homepage with a set of AI‑focused icons and an expandable sidebar that shows recent AI Mode conversations.
The change was announced by Google search vice‑president Robby Stein on X after a weeks‑long test and went live in mid‑November 2026.

entries.text: The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the classic Search button is gone.
The new homepage places three new icons under the query bar: one for image generation, one for file analysis, and one for brainstorming with Gemini, Google’s conversational model.
A gray bar on the left opens a collapsible sidebar that lists prior AI chats, lets users start a new thread, search past threads, or link a Gemini Notebook.
Stein said the sidebar made a “big difference” in how users continue web searches, describing it as a simpler way to pick up where they left off.
Google’s search interface has long featured a permanent Search button, but autocomplete suggestions often hide it, leading most users to press Enter instead.
Usage data apparently showed the button was rarely clicked, prompting the redesign.

Apple is hiring a senior engineering manager to lead development of an AI agent that can operate a Mac, according to a job posting cited by Bloomberg and reported by TechCrunch on 20 November 2026.
The agent is described as able to browse the web, run commands, write and debug code, and call services, all while choosing the appropriate tool for each step.
Apple has not commented on the effort.
The posting says the agent will move fluidly between apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, handling multi‑step tasks across these environments.
Apple plans to roll out the feature in macOS 27.3, which will also add warnings to limit third‑party agents from gaining full system control.
The company aims to introduce the service as early as the end of next year, though development is still in early stages.
AI agents that can use a computer have become a hot commodity, with firms like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Meta launching similar services in the past year.
Apple’s push aligns with its broader AI strategy under senior vice president John Ternus, seeking to expand its assistant capabilities while tightening security for third‑party tools.

Signal announced on 20 November 2026 that it will block screenshots by default on iOS 27 and Android to stop AI assistants from reading messages.
problems: model check: Source gives the article publication date, not an explicit statement that Signal announced the change on that date.

entries.text: The change targets built‑in agents such as Apple’s Siri and Google’s Gemini, which can capture on‑screen content for assistance.
Users can re‑enable screenshots in the app settings, but doing so may expose their chats to those agents.
Signal’s president Meredith Whittaker said the AI agents are “hostile to privacy” and that existing OS tools do not let developers easily block data access without harming user experience.
The screenshot block is a partial fix because AI agents can also read data from the device file system or via deep accessibility permissions used by third‑party tools like Meta’s Muse.
Last year Signal used a similar block to stop Microsoft’s Recall feature from capturing secured chats on Windows 11, showing a pattern of defensive measures against AI‑driven snooping.
The company is urging Apple, Google and Microsoft to provide simple technical controls and clear documentation for developers.
Modern smartphones embed AI assistants that analyze screen content to answer user queries, a function that can inadvertently expose private messages.
Encrypted messaging apps like Signal rely on end‑to‑end encryption, but screen‑capture capabilities bypass that protection by sending visible text to remote servers.
Without OS‑level opt‑out mechanisms, app developers have limited ways to safeguard against such AI‑driven data leakage.
Siri can now read your Signal messages.
